prompt: How do enols behave toward electrophiles?

choices.text: As nucleophiles, because their C=C bonds are electron-rich
As electrophiles, because the oxygen pulls electrons out of the C=C bond
choices.why: The oxygen donates a lone pair by resonance, which makes the double bond more electron-rich, not less.

choices.text: They don't react with electrophiles; only alkenes do
choices.why: Enols react with electrophiles in much the same way that alkenes do.

choices.text: As leaving groups, losing their –OH as hydroxide ion
choices.why: Enols react by attacking an electrophile through the α carbon, not by losing hydroxide.

explanation: Because their double bonds are electron-rich, enols behave as nucleophiles and react with electrophiles in much the same way that alkenes do.

prompt: Why are enols more reactive toward electrophiles than alkenes are?

choices.text: Oxygen's lone pair donates electrons by resonance, making the C=C more electron-rich
The oxygen withdraws electrons inductively, making the C=C more electrophilic
choices.why: Enols react as nucleophiles. Resonance donation from oxygen makes their C=C more electron-rich.

choices.text: Enols carry a negative charge, unlike alkenes
choices.why: Enols are neutral molecules, just as alkenes are.

choices.text: The –OH hydrogen makes the α carbon positively charged
choices.why: The electrostatic potential map of ethenol shows substantial electron density, not positive charge, on the α carbon.

explanation: Because of resonance donation of a lone pair of electrons on the neighboring oxygen, enols are more electron-rich, and correspondingly more reactive, than alkenes.

prompt: The electrostatic potential map of ethenol, H2C=CHOH, shows substantial electron density on which atom?

choices.text: The α carbon, the CH2 carbon
The hydrogen of the –OH group
choices.why: That hydrogen is the one lost at the end of an α-substitution; it isn't electron-rich.

choices.text: The carbon bonded to the –OH group
choices.why: Resonance donation from oxygen builds up electron density on the other carbon of the C=C, the α carbon.

choices.text: No atom; the density is spread evenly over the molecule
choices.why: The map shows a substantial concentration of electron density (yellow-red) on the α carbon.

explanation: The electrostatic potential map of ethenol (H2C=CHOH) shows substantial electron density on the α carbon. That is where an enol attacks an electrophile.

prompt: When an enol reacts with an electrophile, E^+, which step is the same as in an alkene's reaction with E^+?

choices.text: The initial addition of E^+ to the double bond to give a cation
Reaction of the cation with a nucleophile such as a halide ion
choices.why: That second step happens with alkenes, giving an addition product, but not with enols.

choices.text: Loss of the –OH proton from the cation
choices.why: That step is unique to enols; an alkene's cation has no –OH proton to lose.

choices.text: Every step, so both give the same kind of product
choices.why: Only the first step is the same. Alkenes give addition products; enols give α-substituted carbonyl compounds.

explanation: When an alkene reacts with E^+, initial addition gives a cation that then reacts with a nucleophile to give an addition product (Section 7.7). When an enol reacts with E^+, only the initial addition step is the same.

prompt: Instead of adding a nucleophile, what does the cation formed from an enol and an electrophile do?

choices.text: Loses the –OH proton to give an α-substituted carbonyl compound
Adds a halide ion to give an addition product
choices.why: That is what an alkene's cation does. An enol's cation loses H+ instead.

choices.text: Loses a hydrogen from the β carbon to give a new alkene
choices.why: The proton lost is the –OH proton, which regenerates the carbonyl group.

choices.text: Moves the electrophile onto the oxygen to give an enol
choices.why: The electrophile stays on the α carbon, so the product is an α-substituted carbonyl compound.

explanation: In a carbonyl α-substitution reaction (Figure 22.2.1), the enol attacks the electrophile through its α carbon, and the cation intermediate then loses the –OH proton to regenerate a carbonyl group, giving an α-substituted carbonyl compound.
